hook.text: Before stability control, losing grip in a corner often meant spinning out with no way to recover.

buildup.text: ESC uses sensors to compare where you're steering versus where the car is actually going.

discovery.text: If the car slides, ESC brakes individual wheels to pull you back on line—dozens of times per second.

twist.text: Studies show ESC reduces fatal single-vehicle crashes by up to 50%. It's the biggest safety leap since ABS.

climax.text: Since 2012, every new car sold in the US must have it. The technology is now universal.

punchline.text: ESC catches the slides you'd never recover from alone.

quiz.question: How does ESC correct a slide?

details.summary: Electronic stability control detects when a car begins to skid and automatically applies individual brakes and reduces engine power to help the driver maintain control of the vehicle's direction.
details.whyItMatters: ESC has been called the most important safety advance since the seatbelt. Studies show it reduces fatal single-vehicle crashes by up to 50 percent, and it is now mandatory in many countries.
takeaways: Sensors detect the difference between intended and actual direction
Individual brakes are applied to correct the skid automatically
ESC reduces fatal single-vehicle crashes by roughly 50 percent

faq.question: Can you turn off electronic stability control?
faq.answer: Most cars allow partial or full ESC deactivation for situations like driving in deep snow or on a racetrack. However, the system typically reactivates above certain speeds as a safety measure.

faq.question: How does ESC know the car is skidding?
faq.answer: It compares steering wheel angle with data from a yaw rate sensor and wheel speed sensors. If the car is not going where the driver is steering, ESC intervenes to correct the mismatch.
